correctness.rationale: At p=1 the shorter arc from x to y gives a site with distance sum at most max(delta(x,y),1/3): use a site on the arc, or the nearer gap endpoint if the arc is site-free. Every site has distance sum 1/2 at antipodal pairs. This gives R(1)=1/2 and just the antipodal maximizing locus. For p>1, the p-norm is at most the 1-norm, with strict inequality for a site having both coordinate distances positive; such a site exists at every antipodal pair. Compactness makes the pointwise strict bound uniform for each finite p. For the derivative, the uniform norm expansion holds near distance sum 1/2 because u(log u)^j extends continuously at zero and the sum stays positive. Comparing the arc bound with evaluation at an antipodal pair forces maximizing points within O(epsilon) of that locus. In a symmetry interval 0<=x<=1/6, for y=x+1/2+epsilon t the three first-order terms in the interior are -t-H(x), -t-H(1/6-x), t-H(1/3-x), where H is the distance entropy in RESULT.md. At x=0 the stable opposite slopes are from sites 2/3 and 1/3; at x=1/6 they are from sites 0 and 1/3. In both endpoint limits their entropies are H(1/6), so kinks cannot improve the bound. Maximizing the minimum over t gives loss [H(1/3-x)+max(H(x),H(1/6-x))]/2. Symmetry and strict concavity of H show this decreases to x=1/12 and then increases. At the minimizer t=(H(1/4)-H(1/12))/2 attains the common first-order term and the loss is log(12)/4-5 log(5)/24. With r=max(R(p),1/4)<1/2 the product needs at most three closed balls but each factor needs two. The result concerns prescribed centers, not a global three-center optimum; the inspected numerical script was not executed or used as a continuum certificate.
